title_guess: Base effect: the same index rise gives a falling inflation rate
running_examples: January price index: 100 in base year 2012, then 110, 120, 130 in 2013-2015; inflation 10%, 9%, 8.3%

best_moments.why: 10%, 9% and 8.3% sit under three equal 10-point steps, with a curved arc hopping from the 120 cell to the 130 cell: the shrinking percentage from a growing base is visible side by side
the 12-month table collapses to the single January row, so the eye is taken straight to the one comparison that matters

weak_moments.why: about 30 s of a static column of twelve 100s with empty year columns; nothing moves
the formula card sits unchanged for about 28 s; 'base' is never drawn as a thing (for example a rising step or a growing denominator), so the base effect is only numbers

segments.teaches: a price index sets every month of the base year (2012) to 100; later years are read against that 100

elements.what: column of the twelve month names with a blue base-year column that reads 100 in every row
[2012] stamped above the Base Year header
three empty blue year columns 2013, 2014, 2015 added to the right
cream band across the January row ending in a 'Price Index' label

segments.notes: no icons at all; the whole video is one table that is trimmed and annotated
segments.idea: a price index starts at 100 in the base year and later prices are shown as a number against that 100
segments.shown_as: a column of twelve months, each reading 100, pops in under a 'base year' header and 2012 is stamped on top; three empty year columns (2013-2015) slide in beside it; a cream band runs along the January row and ends in a 'Price Index' label

segments.teaches: January's index rises 100 → 110 → 120 → 130; the price index is relative to the base year, while inflation % is relative to the previous year

elements.what: table trimmed to the single January row; 110, 120, 130 fill the year cells
bracket note 'relative to base year' beside the Price Index label
second cream band 'Inflation %' under the row
bracket note 'relative to previous year's index'

segments.notes: the two reference points (base year vs previous year) are only stated in bracket notes, not drawn
segments.idea: an index compares a year with the fixed base year; an inflation rate compares a year with the year just before
segments.shown_as: the other eleven month rows vanish, leaving one January row; 110, 120 and 130 fill the 2013-2015 cells; a bracket note 'relative to base year' is written after the Price Index label, then an empty cream 'Inflation %' row slides in underneath with the note 'relative to previous year'

segments.teaches: inflation % = (this year's index − last year's index) ÷ last year's index × 100; equal 10-point rises give 10%, 9%, 8.3% because the base keeps growing (base effect)

elements.what: pink card hanging from the Inflation % row: (current-year index − previous-year index) / previous-year index × 100, the year words in dark chips
10% under 2013, 9% under 2014, 8.3% under 2015 (last one in a fainter colour)
curved arc from the 120 cell to the 130 cell

segments.notes: formula card appears at 77 s, results only at 106-110 s; the punchline (shrinking %) is carried by three numbers
segments.idea: when the index climbs by the same amount every year, the inflation rate still falls because each year's rise is divided by a bigger previous value
segments.shown_as: a pink formula card pops out of the Inflation % row like a speech bubble (this year minus last year, over last year, × 100); then 10% appears under 2013, 9% under 2014, and a curved arc hops from the 120 cell to the 130 cell as 8.3% appears under 2015: the same 10-point step, a shrinking percentage

segments.teaches: none (channel app promo and next-video card)

elements.what: app promo phone pops up, canvas clears to a next-video / playlist card

segments.shown_as: promo phone slides up over the table, then the canvas is replaced by the channel's next-video card
